bmt-2024-power-01a.title: Construction with 3 folds
bmt-2024-power-01a.body:
1. Fold the left side onto the right side (fold C) and keep the paper folded: the crease is the vertical midline.
2. Fold the (folded) paper in half again, the new crease being the horizontal midline (fold C). The paper is now a stack of four small squares.
3. Fold the small square along a diagonal, i.e. one corner onto the opposite corner (fold B).

Unfolding, the vertical midline, the horizontal midline and, because the stack was reflected across the midlines, both diagonals of the original paper are creased. They cut the paper into $8$ congruent right isosceles triangles.

**Answer: 3 folds.**

bmt-2024-power-01a.title: Why 2 folds are not enough
bmt-2024-power-01a.body: A single fold of the (possibly multi-layer) folded paper is a straight line in the folded picture. Each region of the current crease pattern is one layer of the folded stack, so the new fold line cuts it into at most $2$ pieces. Thus after $k$ folds there are at most $2^k$ regions. For $8$ regions we need $2^k\ge8$, so $k\ge3$. Hence $3$ is the minimum.

bmt-2024-power-01c.title: Pythagoras
bmt-2024-power-01c.body: From Question 1.2, $x=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}l$. Then $x^2+\left(\frac l2\right)^2=\frac34l^2+\frac14l^2=l^2$, so by the converse of the Pythagorean theorem the triangle with sides $x$, $\frac l2$, $l$ is a right triangle with hypotenuse $l$. (It is the $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle scaled by $l$.) $\blacksquare$

bmt-2024-power-01d.title: A concrete triangle
bmt-2024-power-01d.body:
Put the square at $[0,l]^2$ with corner $B=(0,0)$. The arc of radius $l$ about $B$ meets the horizontal midline $y=\frac l2$ at $T=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}l,\frac l2\right)$ (since $\frac34l^2+\frac14l^2=l^2$). Let $F=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2l,0\right)$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $T$ to the bottom side.

Then $BF=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}l$, $FT=\frac l2$, $BT=l$ and the angle at $F$ is a right angle: triangle $BFT$ has the required sides, with its vertices $B$ (corner), $T$ (arc $\cap$ midline) and $F$ (on a side). By symmetry there are many other placements.

bmt-2024-power-01e.title: Fold sequence
bmt-2024-power-01e.body:
Take the paper as $[0,1]^2$ (scale by $l$ otherwise) with $B=(0,0)$, $A=(0,1)$, $C=(1,0)$.

1. Fold left side onto right side (C), crease $x=\frac12$; unfold.
2. Fold bottom side onto top side (C), crease $y=\frac12$; unfold.
3. Fold $A$ onto the line $y=\frac12$ with the crease through $B$ (E). Since $BA=1$, $A$ lands at $T=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2,\frac12\right)$ (distance $1$ from $B$ on the midline). Keep folded.
4. Fold perpendicular to the bottom edge through $T$ (D), crease $x=\frac{\sqrt3}2$. Unfold everything.
5. Fold $C$ onto the line $x=\frac12$ with the crease through $B$ (E): $C$ lands at $T'=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$. Keep folded.
6. Fold perpendicular to the left edge through $T'$ (D), crease $y=\frac{\sqrt3}2$. Unfold.

The creases $x=\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and $y=\frac{\sqrt3}2$ together with the left and bottom edges bound a square of side $\frac{\sqrt3}2$, whose area is $\frac34$ of the original. That is $6\le8$ folds.

bmt-2024-power-01f.title: Maximality
bmt-2024-power-01f.body:
Let an equilateral triangle of side $s$ lie in a unit square. For a direction at angle $\psi$, the width of the triangle in that direction is $s\cdot\max_k|\cos(\psi-\theta_k)|$ where $\theta_k\in\{0^\circ,60^\circ,120^\circ\}$ are the directions of its sides (the width of a convex polygon is the largest projection of its edges). So the horizontal and vertical widths are $s\cos d$ and $s\cos d'$, where $d$ is the angular distance from the horizontal to the nearest side direction and $d'$ is the angular distance from the vertical to the nearest side direction. The side directions $\{0^\circ,60^\circ,120^\circ\}$ and the directions perpendicular to the sides $\{30^\circ,90^\circ,150^\circ\}$ alternate every $30^\circ$, and the horizontal direction lies between a side direction and a perpendicular one; hence $d+d'=30^\circ$ and $\min(d,d')\le15^\circ$.

Fitting in the square needs $s\cos d\le1$ and $s\cos d'\le1$, and $\max(\cos d,\cos d')\ge\cos15^\circ$, so $s\le\sec15^\circ=\sqrt6-\sqrt2$. Equality is attained at $d=d'=15^\circ$: the triangle with a vertex at a corner and the two sides from that vertex at $15^\circ$ to the square's sides. Maximal area: $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}(\sqrt6-\sqrt2)^2=\frac{\sqrt3}4(8-4\sqrt3)=2\sqrt3-3$.

bmt-2024-power-01f.title: Folding it
bmt-2024-power-01f.body:
Take the paper $[0,1]^2$ and the vertex $C=(1,0)$.

1. Fold the vertical midline $x=\frac12$ (C), unfold. 2. Fold the horizontal midline $y=\frac12$ (C), unfold.
3. Fold the top-right corner $(1,1)$ onto the vertical midline with the crease through $C$ (E): the corner lands at $\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$ (distance $1$ from $C$), so the crease makes $15^\circ$ with the right side. It meets the top edge at $Q_1=(\sqrt3-1,1)$; unfold.
4. Fold the bottom-left corner $(0,0)$ onto the horizontal midline with the crease through $C$ (E): the crease makes $15^\circ$ with the bottom side and meets the left side at $Q_2=(0,2-\sqrt3)$; unfold.
5. Fold through $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ (A).

Triangle $CQ_1Q_2$ has $CQ_1=CQ_2=\sec15^\circ$ and angle $60^\circ$ at $C$, so it is the maximal equilateral triangle.

bmt-2024-power-01g.title: Fold sequence
bmt-2024-power-01g.body:
Take the paper as $[0,1]^2$.

1. Fold the vertical midline $x=\frac12$ (C); unfold.
2. Fold through the bottom-left corner $(0,0)$ and the top of the midline $\left(\frac12,1\right)$ (A); unfold. This crease is $y=2x$.
3. Fold along the diagonal from the top-left $(0,1)$ to the bottom-right $(1,0)$ (A or B); unfold. This crease is $y=1-x$.
4. The two creases meet where $2x=1-x$: at $\left(\frac13,\frac23\right)$. Fold perpendicular to the bottom edge through this point (D): the crease $x=\frac13$.
5. Fold the right edge $x=1$ onto the crease $x=\frac13$ (C): the new crease is $x=\frac23$.

The creases $x=\frac13$ and $x=\frac23$ divide the paper into thirds, and only one fold was made at a time. (The triangles formed by the two diagonals through the intersection point are similar with ratio $1:2$, which is why the point $\frac13$ appears.)

bmt-2024-power-01h.title: Perpendicular bisector
bmt-2024-power-01h.body:
The crease $L$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. The slope of $AB$ is $\frac{1-\frac1{2k}}{\frac1{2k}}=2k-1$, and its midpoint is $\left(\frac1{4k},\frac{2k+1}{4k}\right)$. So $L$ has slope $-\frac1{2k-1}$:
$$y-\frac{2k+1}{4k}=-\frac1{2k-1}\left(x-\frac1{4k}\right).$$
At $x=0$: $y=\frac{2k+1}{4k}+\frac{1}{4k(2k-1)}=\frac{(2k+1)(2k-1)+1}{4k(2k-1)}=\frac{4k^2}{4k(2k-1)}=\frac{k}{2k-1}$.

Hence the distance from $P$ to $(0,1)$ is $1-\frac{k}{2k-1}=\frac{k-1}{2k-1}$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2024-power-01i.title: Algorithm
bmt-2024-power-01i.body:
1. Use the given algorithm to divide the left edge into $k$ equal segments, giving $\frac1k$, and bisect (fold B) to get $A=\left(0,\frac1{2k}\right)$. Fold the bottom edge onto the left edge (C) to get the diagonal $y=x$; folding $A$ across it (B) gives $\left(\frac1{2k},0\right)$, and a fold perpendicular to the bottom edge through that point (D) meets the top edge at $B=\left(\frac1{2k},1\right)$.
2. Fold $A$ onto $B$ (B): by Question 1.8 the crease meets the left edge at $P=\left(0,\frac k{2k-1}\right)$.
3. Divide the segment from $(0,0)$ to $P$ into $k$ equal parts with the given algorithm: each has length $\frac1{2k-1}$. Let $P_1=\left(0,\frac1{2k-1}\right)$ be the first division point, and $P_0=(0,0)$.
4. Having $P_{i-2}$ and $P_{i-1}$, fold perpendicular to the left edge through $P_{i-1}$ (D): this horizontal crease is the perpendicular bisector of $P_{i-2}P_i$, so reflecting $P_{i-2}$ over it gives $P_i$, and $P_i=\left(0,\frac i{2k-1}\right)$. Repeating up to $i=a$ gives $P_a=\left(0,\frac a{2k-1}\right)$, i.e. the length $\frac a{2k-1}$ (for $a\le2k-1$, up to the top edge).

bmt-2024-power-01j.title: Induction
bmt-2024-power-01j.body:
**Claim.** For every $n\ge1$ the point $\left(0,\frac1n\right)$ can be constructed.

*Division step.* If $\left(0,\frac1m\right)$ is constructible then any segment $[0,L]$ on the left edge can be divided into $m$ equal parts: fold perpendicular to the edges to get the points $(1,L)$ and $\left(\frac1m,0\right)$ (reflect $\left(0,\frac1m\right)$ over the diagonal), draw the line from $(0,0)$ to $(1,L)$ (A), fold the vertical line $x=\frac1m$ (D) to meet it at $\left(\frac1m,\frac Lm\right)$ and fold horizontally (D) to $\left(0,\frac Lm\right)$. Then repeated reflections (as in Question 1.9, step 4) mark all multiples of $\frac Lm$.

*Induction on $n$.* $n=1$: the corner $(0,1)$. Assume $\frac1m$ is constructible for all $m<n$.
- If $n=2k$ is even, $k<n$, so $\frac1k$ is constructible, and folding $\left(0,\frac1k\right)$ onto $(0,0)$ (B) gives $\frac1{2k}=\frac1n$.
- If $n=2k-1\ge3$ is odd, then $k=\frac{n+1}{2}<n$, so $\frac1k$ is constructible, hence segments can be divided into $k$ equal parts, and Question 1.9 constructs $\frac{1}{2k-1}=\frac1n$.

Finally $\left(0,\frac ab\right)$ is obtained from $\left(0,\frac1b\right)$ by reflecting repeatedly (fold D through $P_{i-1}$ taking $P_{i-2}$ to $P_i$) until $a$ steps. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2024-power-02a.title: A pattern
bmt-2024-power-02a.body:
Take the two diagonals of the square. The only interior vertex is the centre $\left(\frac12,\frac12\right)$, where the four creases (the half-diagonals) meet:
$$V=\left\{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1),\left(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\right)\right\},\quad E=\{\{v_i,v_5\}:i=1,\dots,4\}$$
with $v_1,\dots,v_4$ the corners and $v_5$ the centre. Other answers are possible (e.g. the two midlines).

bmt-2024-power-02b.title: No interior vertices
bmt-2024-power-02b.body: All four vertices lie on the boundary of the square, so there is no interior vertex at which creases must satisfy a local condition; the three creases never cross each other inside the paper. Hence every labelling of the three creases by $\pm1$ is valid. For example, label $\{v_1,v_2\}\mapsto1$, $\{v_2,v_3\}\mapsto-1$, $\{v_2,v_4\}\mapsto1$.

bmt-2024-power-02c.title: Local analysis and the twist
bmt-2024-power-02c.body:
Each of the four interior vertices has four creases and, by the rotational symmetry of the pattern, the same angles $(90^\circ,45^\circ,90^\circ,135^\circ)$ around it (alternating sum $90-45+90-135=0$, so Kawasaki's condition holds). The $45^\circ$ wedge is bordered by two $90^\circ$ wedges, so by the Big-Little-Big lemma the two creases bounding the $45^\circ$ wedge (one inner-square edge and one outgoing crease) have opposite labels. By Maekawa's theorem the four labels at a vertex are split $3:1$, so the other two creases (the other inner-square edge and the other outgoing crease) get the same label.

Choosing all four inner-square edges to be valleys ($+1$), at each vertex the outgoing crease bounding the $45^\circ$ wedge must be a mountain ($-1$) and the other outgoing crease a valley ($+1$). Rotating this choice by $90^\circ$ around the centre is consistent at all four vertices. This is the classical square twist: the central square is rotated while the four surrounding panels pleat flat, and it can be folded (replacing every label by its negative gives the mirror twist). So a valid MV-assignment exists.

bmt-2024-power-02d.title: Up and down
bmt-2024-power-02d.body: Fold the pattern flat. Each face then lies flat either with its original front side up or with its back side up. Two faces sharing a crease are joined by a fold of the paper, which turns the sheet over: one of them is face-up and the other face-down. So colouring "face-up" faces one colour and "face-down" faces the other colour gives a proper 2-colouring.

bmt-2024-power-02e.title: Alternating faces
bmt-2024-power-02e.body: Let the vertex have $d$ creases, so there are $d$ faces around it, in cyclic order $F_1,\dots,F_d$, consecutive faces (including $F_d,F_1$) sharing a crease. In the flat-folded state consecutive faces are on opposite sides (one face-up, one face-down), as in Question 2.4. Going around the vertex the orientation therefore alternates, and after returning to $F_1$ it must be the same as at the start. This happens only if $d$ is even. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2024-power-02f.title: Necessity
bmt-2024-power-02f.body: Suppose the pattern folds flat and take a small circle around the vertex, so that the arc in the $i$-th face has length (proportional to) $\alpha_i$. After folding, the circle maps to a circle around the image of the vertex in the plane, and each face maps by an isometry. Crossing a crease reverses the direction (faces alternate between face-up and face-down), so the image path goes around the image circle through angle $+\alpha_0$, then $-\alpha_1$, then $+\alpha_2$, and so on. The loop closes up, so the net angle travelled, $S=\sum(-1)^i\alpha_i$, is a multiple of $360^\circ$. But $S=\left(\sum\alpha_{\text{even}}\right)-\left(\sum\alpha_{\text{odd}}\right)$ is a difference of two positive numbers whose sum is $360^\circ$, so $|S|<360^\circ$. Hence $S=0$.

bmt-2024-power-02f.title: Sufficiency
bmt-2024-power-02f.body:
Assume $\sum(-1)^i\alpha_i=0$. We prove by induction on $n$ the slightly more general statement for any chain of $2n$ wedges (positive angles, not necessarily summing to $360^\circ$) with alternating sum $0$: it can be folded flat with every crease folded $180^\circ$.

*Base $n=1$:* $\alpha_0=\alpha_1$; the two wedges are mirror images and fold flat along the single crease so they lie on top of each other.

*Step:* let $\alpha_i$ be a smallest angle; then $\alpha_{i-1}\ge\alpha_i$ and $\alpha_{i+1}\ge\alpha_i$. Fold the paper along $l_i$ and $l_{i+1}$ in opposite ways (one mountain, one valley) so that the wedge $W_i$ is tucked as a pleat: in the folded picture $W_i$ lies inside the angular range of $W_{i-1}$ (because $\alpha_i\le\alpha_{i-1}$) and inside that of $W_{i+1}$ (because $\alpha_i\le\alpha_{i+1}$), sandwiched between them in the layer order, so nothing crosses it. After this crimp, the faces $W_{i-1},W_i,W_{i+1}$ act as one wedge of angle $\alpha_{i-1}-\alpha_i+\alpha_{i+1}>0$ and the remaining wedges are unchanged: a chain of $2n-2$ wedges whose alternating sum is still $0$ (the three alternating terms were replaced by their signed combination). By the induction hypothesis the reduced chain folds flat; undoing the crimp (inserting the nested pleat $W_i$) gives a flat folding of the original chain. For the original vertex (total angle $360^\circ$) the chain closes up, so the pattern folds flat. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2024-power-02g.title: Kawasaki plus the full turn
bmt-2024-power-02g.body: Let $E=\sum\alpha_{2i}$ and $O=\sum\alpha_{2i+1}$. Around the vertex the angles add up to a full turn: $E+O=360^\circ$. Kawasaki's theorem (a flat vertex fold has alternating sum $0$) gives $E-O=0$. Adding, $2E=360^\circ$, so $E=180^\circ$ and then $O=180^\circ$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2024-power-02h.title: Turning number of the cross-section
bmt-2024-power-02h.body: Take a small circle $\gamma$ around the vertex. After the flat fold, $\gamma$ becomes a closed curve made of straight pieces (the arcs in the faces, all lying along one circle around the folded vertex, seen edge-on as pieces of a line) joined at the creases; imagine the layers slightly separated so that the curve does not cross itself. At a crease the curve makes a $U$-turn of angle $\pi$: counterclockwise (say) at a mountain fold and clockwise at a valley fold. So the total turning of the closed simple curve is $\pi M-\pi V$ (up to sign depending on orientation). A closed simple curve has total turning $\pm2\pi$ (Hopf's Umlaufsatz). Hence $\pi(M-V)=\pm2\pi$, i.e. $M-V=\pm2$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2024-power-02i.title: Big-Little-Big around the triangle
bmt-2024-power-02i.body:
At each of the three vertices of the equilateral triangle the four angles around the vertex are $60^\circ,90^\circ,120^\circ,90^\circ$ (in cyclic order), the $60^\circ$ angle being the triangle's own angle, flanked by two $90^\circ$ angles. By the Big-Little-Big lemma the two creases bounding the $60^\circ$ angle, which are two sides of the triangle, have opposite labels.

Let the sides be $s_1,s_2,s_3$. Applying this at the three vertices gives $s_1
e s_2$, $s_2
e s_3$, $s_3
e s_1$ (labels in $\{\pm1\}$). But among three labels from a two-element set two must coincide. Contradiction, so no valid MV-assignment exists and the pattern is not flat-foldable.

bmt-2024-power-02j.title: Phantom fold
bmt-2024-power-02j.body: There are three interior vertices, the corners of the triangle. At each the angles in cyclic order are $60^\circ,90^\circ,120^\circ,90^\circ$ (two right angles opposite each other), so $60-90+120-90=0$: Kawasaki's condition holds, and the pattern is a phantom fold. (Equivalently, with the two right angles opposite each other, the other two angles sum to $180^\circ$.)

bmt-2024-power-02j.title: The line graph
bmt-2024-power-02j.body:
Vertices: the triangle sides $s_1$ (base), $s_2$, $s_3$, and the other creases $c_1,c_2$ at the left base vertex, $c_3,c_4$ at the right base vertex, $c_5,c_6$ at the apex.

At each vertex the Big-Little-Big lemma ($60^\circ$ flanked by two $90^\circ$ angles) forces the two triangle sides meeting there to have opposite labels: edges $s_1s_2$, $s_2s_3$, $s_3s_1$, a **triangle**. At the same vertex, Maekawa's theorem requires a $3:1$ split among the four creases; since the two triangle sides are one of each, the other two creases must be equal: forced same parity, so we add a vertex joined to both (paths $c_1-v-c_2$, $c_3-v'-c_4$, $c_5-v''-c_6$).

So $G_L$ is a triangle together with three paths of length $2$; the triangle is an odd cycle, which (Question 2.11) shows that the pattern cannot fold flat.

bmt-2024-power-02k.title: From a valid assignment to a 2-colouring
bmt-2024-power-02k.body:
Suppose $G$ is flat-foldable, with a valid MV-assignment $\mu:E\to\{\pm1\}$. Colour each crease-vertex of $G_L$ by its label $\mu$. Then:
- An edge between two creases forced to have different labels joins vertices of different colours.
- For two creases forced to have the same label $\epsilon$, the added vertex $v_{i,j}$ is adjacent to both; give it the colour $-\epsilon$. Both of its edges are then bichromatic.

So every edge of $G_L$ joins two different colours: $G_L$ is 2-vertex colorable. By contraposition, if $G_L$ is not 2-colorable, $G$ is not flat-foldable. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2024-power-02l.title: Count colourings by component
bmt-2024-power-02l.body:
Valid MV-assignments correspond to proper 2-colourings of $C_L$ (colour of a crease $=$ its label, with the extra vertices coloured as in the previous question). Since $C$ is flat-foldable, at least one exists, so every component of $C_L$ is 2-colorable.

In a connected 2-colourable graph, the colour of one vertex determines the colours of all others (neighbours must differ), and either colour of that vertex is possible by swapping the two colours of a valid colouring. So each component has exactly $2$ colourings. Different components do not constrain each other, so the colourings of the whole graph number $2\cdot2\cdots2=2^n$.

**Answer: $2^n$**

bmt-2024-power-03a.title: Complete to $(x-h)^2=4p(y-k)$
bmt-2024-power-03a.body:
(1) $x^2=1\cdot(y-5)$, so $h=0$, $k=5$, $4p=1$, $p=\frac14$: focus $\left(0,5+\frac14\right)=\left(0,\frac{21}4\right)$, directrix $y=5-\frac14=\frac{19}4$.

(2) $3x^2=16y-32$, so $x^2=\frac{16}{3}(y-2)$: $h=0$, $k=2$, $4p=\frac{16}{3}$, $p=\frac43$. Focus $\left(0,2+\frac43\right)=\left(0,\frac{10}3\right)$, directrix $y=2-\frac43=\frac23$.

bmt-2024-power-03b.title: Equidistance
bmt-2024-power-03b.body: Folding reflects $P$ to $P'$ across the crease $C$, so $C$ is the perpendicular bisector of $PP'$. As $X\in C$, $XP=XP'$. Since $XP'\perp L$ with $P'\in L$, $XP'$ is the distance from $X$ to the line $L$. Thus $X$ is equidistant from $P$ and $L$, so $X\in E$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2024-power-03c.title: Uniqueness
bmt-2024-power-03c.body:
Let $Q\neq X$ be on $C$. As in 3.2, $QP=QP'$. If $QP'$ were perpendicular to $L$, then $Q$ would lie on the perpendicular to $L$ at $P'$; but that line meets $C$ in exactly one point, namely $X$ (it is not parallel to $C$: that would need $C\perp L$, i.e. $PP'\parallel L$, which forces $P\in L$, excluded). So $QP'$ is not perpendicular to $L$, hence $QP'>\mathrm{dist}(Q,L)$ (the perpendicular distance is the shortest). Therefore $QP=QP'>\mathrm{dist}(Q,L)$ and $Q\notin E$.

So $C$ meets $E$ only at $X$, i.e. $C$ is tangent to $E$ at $X$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2024-power-03d.title: Complete the square
bmt-2024-power-03d.body:
$y=x^2+ax+b\iff y-b+\frac{a^2}4=\left(x+\frac a2\right)^2\iff\left(x+\frac a2\right)^2=4\cdot\frac14\left(y-\left(b-\frac{a^2}4\right)\right)$. So $h=-\frac a2$, $k=b-\frac{a^2}4$, $p=\frac14$.

Focus $\left(-\frac a2,\ b-\frac{a^2}{4}+\frac14\right)$; directrix $y=b-\frac{a^2}4-\frac14$.

bmt-2024-power-03e.title: Choose $x=-a/2$
bmt-2024-power-03e.body:
Substituting $x=-\frac a2$ makes the two square-root terms cancel: $y=-\frac a2\sqrt{a^2-4b}+\frac a2\sqrt{a^2-4b}+2b-\frac{a^2}2=2b-\frac{a^2}2$. So $P'=\left(-\frac a2,\,2b-\frac{a^2}{2}\right)$ lies on both tangent creases (for the two roots), and it is constructible from $a$ and $b$ using only the four arithmetic operations (which can be done by folding).

**Finding a root.** Fold the focus $P$ onto the directrix $L$ with the crease passing through $P'$ (fold E; there are two such creases, one for each root). By Theorem 3.3 and the above, each such crease is tangent to the parabola at a root, i.e. at a point of the $x$-axis. So the crease meets the $x$-axis exactly at the root $\frac{-a\pm\sqrt{a^2-4b}}2$ of $x^2+ax+b$.

bmt-2024-power-03f.title: Folding steps
bmt-2024-power-03f.body:
1. Fold through $A$ and $B$ (fold A): the line $AB$.
2. Fold $A$ onto $B$ (fold B): the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. Its intersection with line $AB$ is the midpoint $C$.
3. Fold $A$ onto the $x$-axis with the crease passing through $C$ (fold E). The image $A'$ of $A$ lies on the $x$-axis, and since the crease passes through $C$, $CA'=CA$, so $A'$ lies on the circle with centre $C$ and radius $CA$ (the circle with diameter $AB$). Hence $A'$ is one of the two intersection points of the circle with the $x$-axis, say $M$.
4. The second fold E with the other possible crease through $C$ gives the other intersection point.

bmt-2024-power-03g.title: Equation of the circle
bmt-2024-power-03g.body:
$C=\left(-\frac a2,\frac{1+b}2\right)$ and the radius is $\frac12AB=\frac12\sqrt{a^2+(b-1)^2}$. The circle is
$$\left(x+\frac a2\right)^2+\left(y-\frac{1+b}2\right)^2=\frac14\left(a^2+(b-1)^2\right).$$
At $y=0$: $x^2+ax+\frac{a^2}4+\frac{(1+b)^2}{4}=\frac{a^2}4+\frac{(b-1)^2}{4}$, so $x^2+ax+\frac{(1+b)^2-(b-1)^2}{4}=0$, i.e. $x^2+ax+b=0$. Hence the $x$-coordinates of $M$ and $N$ are exactly the roots. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2024-power-03h.title: Common tangent
bmt-2024-power-03h.body: By Theorem 3.3, a crease that places $A$ onto $r$ is tangent to the parabola with focus $A$ and directrix $r$, and a crease that places $B$ onto $s$ is tangent to the parabola with focus $B$ and directrix $s$. The Beloch fold uses one crease that does both, so it is a line tangent to both parabolas: a common tangent. (Two parabolas generally have up to three common tangents, which is why the Beloch fold solves cubic equations.)

bmt-2024-power-03i.title: Construction
bmt-2024-power-03i.body:
1. **Auxiliary lines.** Fold along $r$ (fold A through two known points of $r$): $A$ lands at $\hat A$, its mirror image in $r$; mark it. Fold through $A$ and $\hat A$ (A): the line $m\perp r$. Fold perpendicular to $m$ through $\hat A$ (D): this is the line $r'$, parallel to $r$, at the same distance from $r$ as $A$ but on the other side. Do the same with $B$ and $s$ to get $s'$.
2. **Beloch fold.** Make the single fold placing $A$ onto $r'$ (at $A'$) and $B$ onto $s'$ (at $B'$). The crease is the perpendicular bisector of $AA'$ and of $BB'$.
3. **Corners $X,Y$.** Since $A$ and $A'$ are at the same distance from $r$ on opposite sides, the midpoint of $AA'$ lies on $r$; call it $X=$ crease $\cap$ line $AA'$, which equals crease $\cap\,r$ (fold A through $A,A'$ to see $X$). Likewise $Y$, the midpoint of $BB'$, lies on $s$, and $Y=$ crease $\cap\ s$. So $X\in r$, $Y\in s$ and both lie on the crease: $XY$ is the crease segment.
4. **Sides through $A$ and $B$.** Line $AA'$ is perpendicular to the crease at $X$; line $BB'$ is perpendicular to it at $Y$. So the lines $XA$ and $YB$ are the perpendiculars to $XY$ at $X$ and $Y$ (fold D through $X$ and through $Y$ to the crease). These are the lines containing the sides $WX$ and $YZ$.
5. **Complete the square.** Fold $Y$ onto the line $XA$ with the crease passing through $X$ (E): $Y$ lands at $W$ with $XW=XY$, on the line of the side through $X$. Fold $X$ onto the line $YB$ with the crease through $Y$ (E): $X$ lands at $Z$ with $YZ=XY$ (choosing the creases so that $W$ and $Z$ are on the same side of $XY$). Fold through $W$ and $Z$ (A).

Then $WXYZ$ has two adjacent sides $XW$ and $YZ$ perpendicular to $XY$ and equal to $XY$: it is a square, with $X\in r$, $Y\in s$, and the sides $WX$, $YZ$ through $A$, $B$ respectively.

bmt-2024-power-03j.title: Folding sequence and similar triangles
bmt-2024-power-03j.body:
1. Construct $r'$ ($x=1$) and $s'$ ($y=2$) as in Question 3.9.
2. Make the Beloch fold: place $A$ onto $r'$ (at $A'$) and $B$ onto $s'$ (at $B'$). The crease $\ell$ meets the $y$-axis at $X$ (the midpoint of $AA'$) and the $x$-axis at $Y$ (the midpoint of $BB'$).

**Why $OX=\sqrt[3]2$.** The line $AA'$ is perpendicular to the crease, as is $BB'$. Thus $AX\perp XY$ and $BY\perp XY$. Let $O$ be the origin. In right triangle $OAX$ (right angle at $O$), $\angle OAX=90^\circ-\angle AXO=\angle OXY$ (because $\angle AXY=90^\circ$), so the right triangles $OAX$ and $OXY$ are similar; in the same way $OXY$ and $OYB$ are similar. Hence
$$\frac{OA}{OX}=\frac{OX}{OY}=\frac{OY}{OB}.$$
With $OA=1$ and $OB=2$: $OX^2=OY$ and $OY^2=2\,OX$, so $OX^4=OY^2=2\,OX$ and $OX^3=2$. Therefore $OX=\sqrt[3]2$, constructed as the distance from the origin to the point where the Beloch crease meets the $y$-axis.

bmt-2024-power-04a.title: Two reflections
bmt-2024-power-04a.body: Fold along the $x$-axis (an existing crease line): the image of $(a,b)$ is $(a,-b)$, which is constructible by Definition 4.1. Now fold along the $y$-axis (also an existing line): the image of $(a,-b)$ is $(-a,-b)$. So $(-a,-b)$ is origami-constructible.

bmt-2024-power-04b.title: Parallelogram
bmt-2024-power-04b.body:
1. Fold through $O=(0,0)$ and $(a,b)$ (A): line $F_1$. 2. Fold through $O$ and $(c,d)$ (A): line $F_2$.
3. Fold perpendicular to $F_2$ through $(a,b)$ (D): line $G$. Fold perpendicular to $G$ through $(a,b)$ (D): this is the line through $(a,b)$ parallel to $F_2$.
4. Repeat with the roles swapped: the line through $(c,d)$ parallel to $F_1$.

The two parallel lines meet at the fourth vertex of the parallelogram with vertices $O$, $(a,b)$, $(c,d)$, which is $(a+c,b+d)$ (since vector sum). Being the intersection of two creases, it is origami-constructible.

bmt-2024-power-04c.title: Similar triangles
bmt-2024-power-04c.body:
First, $(0,1)$ is constructible: fold the $x$-axis onto the $y$-axis (C) to get the line $y=x$ and reflect $(1,0)$ over it.
1. Fold perpendicular to the $x$-axis through $(a,0)$ (D): the line $x=a$.
2. Fold perpendicular to the $y$-axis through $(0,1)$ (D): the line $y=1$. They meet at $(a,1)$.
3. Fold through the origin and $(a,1)$ (A): the line $y=\frac xa$.
4. Fold perpendicular to the $x$-axis through $(1,0)$ (D): the line $x=1$. It meets $y=\frac xa$ at $\left(1,\frac1a\right)$.

Finally, a fold perpendicular to the $y$-axis through $\left(1,\frac1a\right)$ meets the $y$-axis at $\left(0,\frac1a\right)$, so $\left(0,\frac1a\right)$ is origami-constructible.

bmt-2024-power-04d.title: Slope $a$
bmt-2024-power-04d.body:
1. Fold the vertical line $x=1$ (D, perpendicular to the $x$-axis through $(1,0)$) and the horizontal line $y=a$ (D, perpendicular to the $y$-axis through $(0,a)$); they meet at $(1,a)$.
2. Fold through the origin and $(1,a)$ (A): the line $y=ax$.
3. Fold perpendicular to the $x$-axis through $(b,0)$ (D): the line $x=b$.

The lines $y=ax$ and $x=b$ meet at $(b,ab)$, which is therefore origami-constructible.

bmt-2024-power-04e.title: Find it and show it is irreducible
bmt-2024-power-04e.body:
Let $\alpha=\sqrt2+\sqrt3$. Then $\alpha^2=5+2\sqrt6$, so $(\alpha^2-5)^2=24$, i.e. $\alpha^4-10\alpha^2+1=0$. So $f(x)=x^4-10x^2+1$ has $\alpha$ as a root.

**Minimality.** It suffices to show $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$ (then it is the minimal polynomial, being monic with $\alpha$ as a root).
- No rational roots: by the rational root theorem the candidates are $\pm1$, and $f(\pm1)=-8\neq0$.
- No factorisation into two rational quadratics $(x^2+ax+b)(x^2+cx+d)$: comparing coefficients, $a+c=0$, $b+d+ac=-10$, $ad+bc=0$, $bd=1$. From $c=-a$ and $ad+bc=a(d-b)=0$: either $a=0$ or $b=d$. If $a=0$ then $b+d=-10$, $bd=1$, so $b$ is a root of $t^2+10t+1$, with discriminant $96$ not a rational square: impossible. If $b=d$ then $b^2=1$, $b=\pm1$ and $b+d-a^2=-10$ gives $a^2=10+2b\in\{12,8\}$, not squares of rationals: impossible.

So $f$ is irreducible, and the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt2+\sqrt3$ is $x^4-10x^2+1$.

**Answer: $x^4-10x^2+1$**

bmt-2024-power-04f.title: Induction on the tower
bmt-2024-power-04f.body:
**Facts used.** (i) $\mathcal O$ is a subfield of $\mathbb C$ containing $\mathbb Q$ and $i$. (ii) $\mathcal O$ is closed under square roots: for a complex $z=re^{i\theta}$, $\sqrt z=\sqrt r\,e^{i\theta/2}$, where $\sqrt r$ comes from a right-triangle (geometric mean) construction and the half-angle by bisecting an angle. (iii) $\mathcal O$ is closed under cube roots: $z^{1/3}=r^{1/3}e^{i\theta/3}$, where $r^{1/3}$ is the real cube root (a root of $x^3-r$, constructible by Theorem 3.6) and $\cos(\theta/3)$ is a root of $4x^3-3x-\cos\theta=0$ (angle trisection, Theorem 3.6), after which $\sin(\theta/3)=\sqrt{1-\cos^2(\theta/3)}$.

**Claim.** $F_k\subseteq\mathcal O$ for all $k$. Base: $F_0=\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathcal O$. Step: assume $F_{k-1}\subseteq\mathcal O$. Because $[F_k:F_{k-1}]$ is $2$ or $3$ (a prime), any $\beta\in F_k\setminus F_{k-1}$ generates $F_k=F_{k-1}(\beta)$ and its minimal polynomial $f$ over $F_{k-1}$ has degree $[F_k:F_{k-1}]=2$ or $3$ with coefficients in $F_{k-1}\subseteq\mathcal O$. Then $\beta$ is given by the quadratic formula (degree 2) or by Cardano's formula (degree 3), which uses only field operations, square roots and cube roots of elements of $\mathcal O$; by (i)-(iii), $\beta\in\mathcal O$. Every element of $F_k=F_{k-1}(\beta)$ is a polynomial in $\beta$ with coefficients in $F_{k-1}\subseteq\mathcal O$, hence lies in the field $\mathcal O$. So $F_k\subseteq\mathcal O$.

By induction $F_n\subseteq\mathcal O$, so $\alpha\in F_n$ is origami-constructible. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2024-power-04g.title: Reduce to roots of unity
bmt-2024-power-04g.body:
A regular $n$-gon can be constructed exactly when its vertices, e.g. the $n$th roots of unity $1,\zeta_n,\dots,\zeta_n^{n-1}$ (with $\zeta_n=e^{2\pi i/n}$), are origami-constructible. Since $\mathcal O$ is a field, this holds iff $\zeta_n\in\mathcal O$. The splitting field of $x^n-1$, and of the minimal polynomial $\Phi_n$ of $\zeta_n$ over $\mathbb Q$, is $\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)$ (all roots of $\Phi_n$ are powers of $\zeta_n$), and $[\mathbb Q(\zeta_n):\mathbb Q]=\deg\Phi_n=\varphi(n)$. By Theorem 4.8,
$$\text{the regular }n\text{-gon is constructible}\iff\varphi(n)=2^a3^b\text{ for some }a,b\ge0.$$

bmt-2024-power-04g.title: When is $arphi(n)=2^a3^b$?
bmt-2024-power-04g.body:
Write $n=\prod q_j^{e_j}$ (distinct primes $q_j$). Then $\varphi(n)=\prod q_j^{e_j-1}(q_j-1)$.

($\Leftarrow$) Let $n=2^a3^bp_1\cdots p_k$ with distinct Pierpont primes. Then $\varphi(n)=2^{a-1}\cdot\left(2\cdot3^{b-1}\right)\cdot\prod(p_i-1)$ (with the obvious modifications if $a=0$ or $b=0$): each factor $p_i-1=2^{a_i}3^{b_i}$, so $\varphi(n)$ is of the form $2^{a'}3^{b'}$ and the $n$-gon is constructible.

($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $\varphi(n)=2^a3^b$. Let $q\ge5$ be a prime dividing $n$.
- If $q^2\mid n$ then $q\mid\varphi(n)$, impossible since $\varphi(n)$ has only the prime factors $2,3$. So $q\,\|\,n$.
- The factor $q-1$ divides $\varphi(n)$, so $q-1=2^{c}3^{d}$: $q=2^c3^d+1>3$ is a Pierpont prime.

The primes $2$ and $3$ may divide $n$ to any power (they contribute $2^{e-1}$ and $2\cdot3^{e-1}$). So $n=2^a3^bp_1\cdots p_k$ with distinct Pierpont primes $p_i$. $\blacksquare$

(For example $n=5=2^2+1$, $7=2\cdot3+1$, $13$, $17$, $19$ are Pierpont primes, while $11$ is not, since $10=2\cdot5$: the regular $11$-gon is the smallest that is not origami-constructible.)
